entries.clue: Pure actions, properly organised safeguards (11)

indicatorNotes.properly organised: the letters are to be put into proper order

annotation.surface: Someone praising deeds done with clean hands and sound planning.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as moral approval, but 'pure actions' is just eleven letters waiting to be rearranged into the plural noun at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Precautions are measures taken in advance to protect against harm, which is what safeguards are.

entries.clue: With which writer makes a point? (6,9)

annotation.definition: With which writer makes a point?

blocks.note: the writer looks like an author, but it is the writing implement itself
not arguing a case: literally putting a sharp tip on something

annotation.surface: A question about the tool a writer uses to argue a case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Makes a point' suggests arguing persuasively; here it is literal, putting a sharp tip on a pencil, and 'writer' is the pencil itself rather than an author.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: the gadget is described by what it does to a writing tool, with the idiom 'make a point' taken literally.

entries.clue: Additional bit of text rarely seen (5)

indicatorNotes.bit of: the answer is only a piece of the words that follow
indicatorNotes.seen: the answer can be seen sitting in plain view within the text

annotation.surface: A snippet of writing that hardly ever gets read, like an appendix.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seen' finishes the surface; the letters sit across the join of 'text' and 'rarely'.
annotation.definitionFit: Extra and additional both mean over and above what is usual.

entries.clue: One lacks a full compliment of members (7)

annotation.definition: One lacks a full compliment of members

blocks.note: reads as a club short of its complete complement (the printed 'compliment' is the setter's spelling)
members also means limbs, arms and legs

annotation.surface: A club or committee that is short of people.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Members' sounds like a club's membership but means limbs. 'Compliment' is the printed spelling; the phrase intended is 'full complement', a complete set.
annotation.definitionFit: An amputee has had a limb removed, so lacks the full set of arms and legs.

entries.clue: As you’d expect to see in pretty pic always (7)

indicatorNotes.to see in: the answer is visible inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: Someone saying a pretty picture is what they always expect to find.
annotation.walkthrough: The letters span three words; 'pic' is doing double duty as a fragment rather than a photograph.
annotation.definitionFit: Typical describes what is usual, just as you would expect.

entries.clue: Old scoundrel coming to old port with something sung (8)

indicatorNotes.coming to: the first pair of pieces is placed next to the port

blocks.note: Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian port

annotation.surface: An aged villain arriving in a harbour with a song on his lips.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the wordplay to the definition, which sits at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: An oratorio is a large choral work, so something sung.

entries.clue: Working on stage and giving background information (7,3,5)

blocks.note: arranging the scenery on a stage

annotation.surface: A stagehand who also explains the story's context.
annotation.walkthrough: The same phrase serves in its literal theatre sense and in its everyday figurative one.
annotation.definitionFit: Setting the scene means both arranging a stage set and supplying context before a story.

entries.clue: Criticises Scottish reformer audibly (6)

indicatorNotes.audibly: we want the word that sounds like the reformer

blocks.note: John Knox, leader of the Scottish Reformation

annotation.surface: A complaint that someone loudly attacks a Scottish religious reformer.
annotation.walkthrough: John Knox was the 16th-century Protestant preacher who led the Reformation in Scotland.
annotation.definitionFit: To knock something is to criticise it, as in knocking a plan.

entries.clue: Small earthquake upsetting Italian capital after short time, right? (6)

indicatorNotes.upsetting: to upset something is to knock it over and disorder it, so the letters are jumbled
indicatorNotes.after: placed after means the jumbled capital comes later in the answer than the short time

blocks.note: T = time, shortened to its abbreviation

annotation.surface: A news question about whether a minor quake has shaken Rome.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' reads as the quake distressing Rome, but it tells you to scramble the city's letters; in a down clue it tempts a reversal, which gives the wrong order.
annotation.definitionFit: A tremor is a slight shaking of the ground, a small earthquake.

entries.clue: No points sadly, with one missing out all the time (7)

indicatorNotes.sadly: the letters are in a sorry state, so rearrange them
indicatorNotes.with one missing: one = I, which is taken away

blocks.note: one = I, removed from the fodder

annotation.surface: A lament over a team scoring nothing because a player is missing.
annotation.walkthrough: Remove I from NO POINTS, then rearrange the seven letters left.
annotation.definitionFit: Nonstop means continuously, happening all the time.

entries.clue: Old magistrate altered a report (7)

annotation.surface: A judge of old doctoring an official report.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests corruption on the bench, but 'altered' is only telling you to shuffle 'a report'.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical office: the title belonged to judicial officials of ancient Rome, hence 'old'.

entries.clue: Concerned with intense experience regarding long-term weather keeping cold (9)

indicatorNotes.keeping: the outer word holds the other inside it

blocks.note: C = cold, as on a tap; goes inside CLIMA_TIC

annotation.surface: A study of extreme weather events and the cold snaps within them.
annotation.walkthrough: CLIMATIC and CLIMACTIC are often confused; the extra C is exactly the cold that is kept inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Climactic describes the climax, the most intense point of an experience.

entries.clue: One has little hesitation after work to get drug (5)

indicatorNotes.after: coming after something means following it, so the one with its hesitation is written behind the work

annotation.surface: Someone who hesitates only briefly after work before taking a drug.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work' is the crossword's usual musical opus, abbreviated as in a catalogue number; 'has' simply glues the hesitation to the one.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the poppy narcotic is one particular drug.

entries.clue: Realise American has boarded ship (4)

indicatorNotes.has boarded: to board a ship is to go inside it

annotation.surface: Discovering that a US passenger has come aboard.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is informal British slang, as in 'I've got him sussed'.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: British informal speech uses it for working something out, the sense of 'realise' here.

entries.clue: One of those knowing the ropes in church? (4,6)

annotation.definition: One of those knowing the ropes in church?

blocks.clueFragment: One of those knowing the ropes
blocks.note: the idiom for someone experienced, who knows how things work
a church tower has real ropes hanging from its bells

annotation.surface: A question about an experienced churchgoer who knows how things work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knowing the ropes' is an idiom for being experienced; here the ropes are real bell ropes.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by activity: those who sound church bells work by pulling ropes, so they literally know the ropes.

entries.clue: Moments when example is read out (8)

indicatorNotes.read out: spoken aloud, so we want a sound-alike

annotation.surface: The moments in class when a worked example is recited.
annotation.walkthrough: 'When' only links the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Instants are very brief moments of time.

entries.clue: Female uncertain about God? That is symptomatic (10)

blocks.note: an agnostic holds that God's existence cannot be known

annotation.surface: A woman who is unsure about religion, described as though her doubt were a symptom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That is' reads like the abbreviation IE but here it merely links the parts.
annotation.definitionFit: Diagnostic features are symptomatic, characteristic of a particular condition.

entries.clue: One very quiet, outwardly boring and a bit wet (6)

indicatorNotes.outwardly: the boring word sits on the outside of the others

blocks.note: dry = dull, boring; it goes round the rest
pp = pianissimo, very quiet in music

annotation.surface: Someone who is quiet and dull, and rather feeble into the bargain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wet' in British slang means feeble or soppy, not damp, so the definition is about character; pp is the musical marking pianissimo.
annotation.definitionFit: Drippy means weak and sentimental, a bit wet.

entries.clue: Hide in prosperous region somewhere in the Med (7)

blocks.note: the South East of England, its wealthiest region

annotation.surface: Someone hiding away in a wealthy corner of the Mediterranean.
annotation.walkthrough: The South East, around London, is Britain's richest region, hence 'prosperous region' for SE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the less common sense of the verb, stowing something out of sight rather than oozing.

entries.clue: Most stupid,like a feathered friend laying an egg? (7)

annotation.definition2: like a feathered friend laying an egg?

blocks.clueFragment: like a feathered friend laying an egg?
blocks.note: where a bird is when it lays: read as three short words

annotation.surface: Calling something the silliest thing, like a bird fussing over an egg.
annotation.walkthrough: Split the answer as IN A NEST for the second, whimsical definition; the question mark flags it.
annotation.definitionFit: Inanest is the superlative of inane, meaning silliest or most stupid.

entries.clue: Resist Sergeant Major’s demand (4)

blocks.note: the parade-ground order to stand still, 'attention!' clipped to its last syllable

annotation.surface: A soldier refusing to obey the parade-ground order.
annotation.walkthrough: On the parade ground 'Attention!' is barked as ''Shun!', and the surface's resisting soldier hides that both halves are the same word.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a verb for avoiding or rejecting something, and the drill sergeant's shortened 'attention!'.

entries.clue: Condition of bare folk, terribly untidy (6)

indicatorNotes.terribly: the letters are in a terrible mess

annotation.surface: A disapproving remark on the scruffy state of naturists.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Untidy' is the very word being rearranged, while it seems to describe the folk.
annotation.definitionFit: Nudity is the state of being naked, the condition of bare people.

entries.clue: Home place for stuff entering (5)

annotation.surface: A spot at home for storing things as they come in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Home' gives IN, as in 'staying in'.
annotation.definitionFit: Input is material that is fed or entered into a system.

entries.clue: His cadets being naughty may be punished (9)

indicatorNotes.being naughty: the letters misbehave and move out of order

annotation.surface: A warning that an officer's misbehaving trainees could be disciplined.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a coherent scene, which hides that 'his cadets' is just the letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word covers rebuking as well as physical punishment, both matching 'punished'.

entries.clue: The short boy gets pound (5)

indicatorNotes.short: the word loses its last letter

annotation.surface: A little lad receiving a pound coin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like money but is the verb: to beat heavily, as a heart does.
annotation.definitionFit: To throb is to pound rhythmically, as a heartbeat or headache does.

entries.clue: Act of contrition in Cornish location – character at the end released (7)

indicatorNotes.released: the named letter is let go from the word

blocks.note: Penzance, a town in Cornwall, south-west England
Z, the character at the end of the alphabet, is removed

annotation.surface: Someone doing penance in a Cornish town before being set free.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character at the end' sounds like the last letter of PENZANCE, which is E; it means the last letter of the alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: Penance is an act performed to show sorrow for sin, an act of contrition.

entries.clue: Serious listener at front of home (7)

indicatorNotes.at front of: the first piece goes before the second

blocks.note: a nest is a bird's home

annotation.surface: A grave-faced person listening at the front door.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Listener' seems to be a person but is the organ that does the listening.
annotation.definitionFit: Earnest means sincere and serious in manner.

entries.clue: Trustworthy creeps about to join the board (11)

indicatorNotes.about: the letters are turned about into a new order

blocks.note: a board is a table, as in bed and board

annotation.surface: Unpleasant people with a veneer of trust about to be made company directors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'on the point of' before 'to join', but it is the anagram indicator acting on 'creeps'.
annotation.definitionFit: Respectable people are regarded as decent and trustworthy.
